newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Rio de Janeiro hosts orchid extravaganza.
newsitem.headline: Rio de Janeiro hosts orchid extravaganza.

text.p: Orchid lovers from around the world on Tuesday descended on Rio de Janeiro to admire the blaze of colours and graceful shapes of more than one million orchid blossoms at the Museum of Modern Art.
Some 5,000 orchid fans, growers, traders and scientists were expected to visit the 15th World Orchid Conference that opened in Rio and runs through Sunday.

Like every show, this one also has its star. Of the 100,000 orchid plants from five continents on display, a white Brazilian cattleya nobilior was crowned grand champion by the panel of 300 judges for its symmetry, colour and petal size.

Orchid lovers attribute the fascination with orchids, which derive their name from the Greek word for testicle because of the shape of some of the flowers, to their huge variety and their ability to be crossbred and generate new specimens.

"I have been raising orchids for 50 years and there is not a moment of dullness," said Jean Inouye from Hawaii, one of the conference judges. "I started with one orchid and now I have about 5,000 plants. There are so many varieties, there is no end to collecting orchids."

The love for orchids also feeds an international $10 billion a year business. An orchid plant, which takes five to seven years until it produces its first flower, can cost up to $1,000, according to Carlos de Gouveia, the coordinator of the conference's judging panel.
Holland leads in world orchid trade with sales worth $4 billion a year followed by Thailand and Malaysia with sales of $2 billion a year each, Gouveia said.
However, South America is the real orchid haven with the largest number of orchid species found in Colombia, then Ecuador and Brazil. Colombia alone boasts some 5,000 different varieties of orchids.
But like many plants and animals, orchids are threatened and some species have already been lost forever, said South African judge Doug McMurtry.
"Orchid habitats are shrinking and growers are breeding more plants to prevent more orchids from being taken from the wild," McMurtry said.
